paragraphs.text:
For the ideal spring system discussed earlier, and for a pendulum in the small-angle approximation, free oscillations can be described as simple harmonic motion when resistive forces are neglected.
The restoring action must also satisfy the models used earlier. "No friction" is not a sufficient condition for every kind of free oscillation to be simple harmonic.
In actual oscillations, friction, air resistance, and other effects often oppose the motion.
Even when these resistive forces are small, they gradually change the energy and amplitude of the oscillations.

For the oscillating system considered here, with no continuing external driving force, resistive forces do negative work. The system's mechanical energy is gradually converted into internal energy of the system and the surrounding medium.
Energy does not disappear. Rather, the mechanical energy available for back-and-forth motion decreases.
When damping is weak and the object still moves back and forth through the equilibrium position, its maximum displacement from equilibrium, or amplitude, gradually decreases with time.

This underdamped motion is the damped oscillation shown by the graph in this lesson.
With greater resistance, the system may instead approach equilibrium directly, without continuing to oscillate back and forth.
Thus, not every motion with resistance can be drawn as a wave whose amplitude gradually shrinks.

In an experiment, saying that oscillations have "stopped" may simply mean that their amplitude has become too small to distinguish.
Different friction mechanisms may lead to different final stopping processes. A schematic diagram alone cannot establish a single exact stopping time for all of them.

While the object still moves back and forth, its damped displacement-versus-time curve can be represented schematically as in Figure $16$.
The amplitude in the figure gradually decreases, but the curve is a schematic, not a measurement record from which to read an exact period, decay rate, or stopping time.
Figure $8$ introduces the recording method and apparatus using a pendulum containing sand.

According to the original book, attaching a piece of stiff paper to the suspension string to increase air resistance allows this method to record the type of decaying curve described above.
The trace already shown in the apparatus drawing does not thereby become an exact damped-oscillation curve.

The original book gives ammeters and wattmeters as examples of electrical measuring instruments with pointers.
When such an instrument is switched on, its pointer may oscillate about the equilibrium position corresponding to the measured value. It takes some time to settle enough for a convenient reading.
To shorten the wait, a special device can provide a suitable amount of damping for the pointer.

In this process, the mechanical energy of the pointer's motion is dissipated as internal energy, not simply eliminated.
Merely placing a stationary metal plate in a magnetic field does not by itself mean that these damping currents will be continuously induced.

As a car travels over an uneven road, the road's continuing action can excite oscillations of the car body.
Shock absorbers reduce these oscillations. Not all oscillations of a moving vehicle can be treated as free oscillations subject only to resistance, nor is the body guaranteed to remain completely still.
The hydraulic shock absorber described in the original book has a piston connected to the car body, moving inside a cylinder filled with liquid.
